Lodz Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Łódź, Poland

Demolished. Jewish settlement in Łódź developed from the late 18th century, with industrialist Izrael Poznański among its leading figures; by 1921, 156,155 Jews (35%) were mostly murdered at Kulmhof and Auschwitz-Birkenau between 1942-1944 (a Jewish community persists in Łódź today). This cemetery, established in 1811 outside the then-city limits, expanded to about 3 hectares before urban development forced its 1892 closure (though occasional funerals continued afterward). By 1938, when a memorial book about the cemetery was published, it held 3,871 tombstones (with actual burials likely far exceeding that count); the mortuary was repurposed as a shelter for the mentally ill. During WWII, the site fell within the Łódź Ghetto and became a German-ordered timber yard in 1942. Postwar, a 1949 road project cut through the grounds, followed by apartment construction; only a wall fragment and two tombstone pieces survive today. In 2008, tram-line construction near Zachodnia Street required protective structural work around remaining nearby graves.
